To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the expression of genes that are involved in cell growth, cell cycle, cell adhesion, and cell signaling pathways are altered in NSCLC, that the expression of these genes is associated with clinical parameters such as stage and survival, and that the expression of a subset of these genes is also associated with response to chemotherapy and survival.
the expression levels of 12 genes, including 6 oncogenes and 6 tumor suppressor genes, were significantly different in pathologic Stage I NSCLC compared with adjacent normal lung tissues.
the expression of 2, 4, 5, 6, and 7 were significantly higher in lung cancer tissues than that in normal lung tissues.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the molecular mechanisms of lung cancer.
the development of new methods for the analysis of gene expression data.
the study of the effects of the environment on the development of the human body, and in particular on the growth of the lungs.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the current evidence supports the use of the following drugs in the treatment of advanced non-small cell lung carcinoma: cisplatin and etoposide, vinorelbine, docetaxel, gemcitabine and paclitaxel.
the use of the term "non-small cell lung cancer" (NSCLC) is justified.
the use of a combination of a number of different methods is the best way to identify and characterize genes involved in the pathogenesis of lung cancer.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we are able to detect and quantify gene expression changes in pathologic Stage I nonsmall cell lung cancers (NSCLCs) that are predictive for survival, and that we can detect and quantify gene expressions that are predictive for recurrence.
the results of our cDNA microarray analysis suggest that there is a distinct pattern of gene expression in Stage IA lung carcinomas.
the results of our cDNA microarray analysis are consistent with a model in which the majority of nonsmall cell lung cancers (NSCLCs) arise from a small number of precursor lesions.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the expression of genes that encode proteins involved in the cell cycle, cell proliferation, apoptosis, and cell signaling is altered in NSCLC.

the majority of the genes that are expressed in lung tumors are expressed in normal lung tissue, which makes it difficult to identify genes that are specifically associated with the development of lung cancer.
there is a significant association between the expression of the gene for a protein called PDL1 and the prognosis of patients with early stage lung cancer.
